hints.title: Audit the operations in order
hints.body: For each transition, name the operation and state why it follows from the assumptions. You can check a claimed algebraic identity by expanding both sides; other deductions need their own reasons.
hints.recap: An identity and an inference from an identity are different kinds of claim.
hints.pitfall: The theorem is stated to be true; that does not establish the validity of this particular argument.
hints.pause: Check the transitions in order without assuming that a later contradiction validates earlier steps.

recall.reminder: An identity and an inference from an identity are different kinds of claim.

hints.title: Test the rule behind a deduction
hints.body: Replace complicated expressions in a suspected inference by simple letters. Then test the resulting general rule with small positive integers, preserving any ordering conditions used in that inference.
hints.recap: One permitted failure can show that a proposed general algebraic rule is not valid.
hints.pitfall: A test of a local algebraic rule is not a proposed solution of the original theorem.
hints.pause: Construct and check your own numerical test, identify which deduction it concerns, and justify every earlier transition.

recall.reminder: One permitted failure can show that a proposed general algebraic rule is not valid.

solution:
Line I is a valid rearrangement. Line II is also valid, since expanding (c−b)(c2+cb+b2) gives c3−b3.

Line III is the first unsupported step. From a·a2=(c−b)(c2+cb+b2), it does not follow that the first factors are equal and the second factors are equal. Even putting each pair in increasing order does not justify this: 6·36=3·72, although 6≠3 and 36≠72.

This numerical example exposes the invalid factor-matching rule; it is not a proposed solution of a3+b3=c3. The proof needs a reason that its particular factors must match, and supplies none. Its later contradiction therefore does not establish the theorem. The first mistake is on line III: D.
knowledgePattern: Reject unjustified matching of factors in an attempted contradiction proof
